background.definition: Encopresis is the repeated involuntary or intentional passage of feces in inappropriate places, such as into clothing or on the floor, in children past the age of toilet training (usually 4 years of age or a mental age of >4 years in developmentally delayed children). Subtypes include retentive encopresis which is far more common and associated with functional constipation and overflow incontinence, and non-retentive encopresis, which is included in the child/adolescent Rome IV criteria as a functional gastrointestinal disorder. Non-retentive encopresis is present in about 20% of cases and is not associated with constipation or overflow incontinence.

list.listitem: The prevalence of encopresis is 4% in preschool-age children and 1% to 2% in otherwise healthy school-age children. A city population study in Norway found an encopresis prevalence rate of 6.4% among 4-year-olds.
A study in Sri Lanka found a prevalence of fecal incontinence in 2% of children (boys 3.2%, girls 0.9%).
In a case series of 270 children with chronic constipation seen by pediatric gastroenterologists, 41 (35%) girls and 76 (65%) boys had overflow incontinence.
In a case series of children with idiopathic constipation and a mean age of 8.2 years (range 1-20 years), 160 patients (74%) had associated encopresis.
Male to female ratio is 3:1 overall; non-retentive encopresis has a male to female ratio of 4:1.

Children with Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have an increased prevalence of constipation (4.1% of children with ADHD vs. 1.5% children without ADHD) and fecal incontinence (0.9% of children with ADHD vs. 0.15% of children without ADHD).

Similarly, psychiatric comorbidities are often seen among children with bladder and bowel dysfunction. In a cross-sectional study of 61 children with bladder and bowel dysfunction seen in urology clinics, 43% had a pre-existing learning disability and 29% reported ADHD.
Among children with functional non-retentive fecal incontinence, urinary incontinence is present in up to half.

Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) have an increased prevalence of functional defecation disorder compared to otherwise healthy children. In a study of 242 children in a specialized outpatient clinic, 29% of children presenting with a functional defecation disorder had concomitant ASD symptoms.

Large diameter stools are painful to pass and the fecal retention cycle continues.
Loose stool can leak around the fecal impaction in the dilated rectum, causing encopresis.

In one study, investigators found defects in neuromuscular control of defecation in children with constipation and encopresis compared to children with constipation alone. These included higher time to maximum relaxation, time to recovery to baseline pressure, and duration of relaxation.

In a case series of 270 children with chronic constipation, onset of constipation after age 2 years, longer duration of constipation, male gender, a history of stool retention, and presence of a hardened fecal mass were associated with encopresis. Among the 117 children with encopresis, chronic constipation appeared later (median age of 30 and 33 months vs. 16 and 12 months in non-encopretic girls and boys, respectively).
Keeping a stool diary (e.g., for 14 days) may help to obtain reliable information on circumstances around soiling.

If the diagnosis is uncertain, administration of the Virginia Ecopresis-Constipation Apperception Test or, for children with intellectual disabilities, the Profile of Toileting Issues can be considered.
See "Diagnostic Testing" in chapter on constipation in children.

In children with functional non-retentive fecal incontinence, the International Children’s Continence Society notes that determination of colonic transit time using abdominal x-ray after ingestion of radiopaque markers, or by colonic transit scintigraphy, is the only useful test to consider; they do not recommend abdominal x-ray alone. Transit time is delayed in about half of children with associated constipation and about 10% in children with functional fecal incontinence.
Plain abdominal x-ray may be useful to rule out fecal retention when the rectal examination is negative for fecal impaction.

In a case series of 215 children with idiopathic constipation, of whom 160 had encopresis, a protocol of a bowel clean-out, administered for 67 children, followed by senna at an average dose of 67 mg (range 5-175 mg) achieved success in 84%. Success was defined as daily fecal evacuation and no soiling. 12 of the remaining 34 children had continued soiling.
Fiber is beneficial in the treatment of constipation with and without encopresis in children.
Use of oral laxatives is not indicated in children with functional non-retentive fecal incontinence.
Use of long-acting methylphenidate had a positive effect on encopresis in 21 children and adolescents with coexisting ADHD.

Antegrade continence enema is a procedure that includes creation of a stoma from native tissue, such as the appendix, that extends from the navel into the large bowel. A catheter is passed through the stoma into the bowel and, once daily, an enema is administered or self-administered. In a case series of 42 patients with severe constipation, 79% with encopresis, use of daily antegrade continence enemas reduced the encopresis rate to 5% and admissions for clean-out from 52% to 19%; improvement in the bowel regimens was observed in 79%. High volume saline flushes were the preferred enema solution.

Sacral nerve stimulation (SNS) is an option for those with a weak but structurally intact anal sphincter. The procedure is usually performed following demonstration of benefit from use of a percutaneous peripheral nerve electrode attached to an external stimulator. The procedure involves electric current applied to one of the sacral nerves via an electrode placed through the corresponding sacral foramen.

In a systematic review of 6 case series of SNS with 266 patients, commissioned by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, most patients experienced a decrease of 50% or more in the number of incontinence episodes and complete continence was achieved in 41% to 75% of patients.

Behavioral training for the patient and family are beneficial. In a meta-analysis of 4 studies, behavioral intervention was more effective than control conditions for author-defined success and soiling frequency; evidence is limited.
Keeping a chart or calendar of stool production (time, amount, location, and consistency) can be helpful in detecting relapse and in suggesting times for successful toileting attempts.
Positive toileting routines (regular toilet sits for 5-10 minutes 3-4 times/day) should be developed.
Attempting defecation 5 to 20 minutes after eating may help take advantage of the gastrocolic reflex.
Demonstrate proper toileting position (upper body flexed slightly at the hips, use of proper foot support).
In a review of 7 studies of encopresis over the past 15 years, only biofeedback and enhanced toilet training were identified as probably efficacious.

For children with combined bladder and bowel dysfunction, various forms of urotherapy, including education, behavior modification, dietary and water intake guidance with or without specific measures such as pelvic floor muscle training and electrostimulation can be useful in resolving encopresis. Authors of a systematic review found resolution rates of encopresis in 20% to 22% of cases.

In a trial of 26 children with non-retentive fecal soiling, children randomized to a psychomotor approach (play therapy) in addition to toilet training for 6 months experienced a greater reduction in episodes of encopresis (from 20 episodes per month to 6.5 (SD ± 1.3) episodes/month vs. 12.0 (SD ± 1.3) for those with toilet training alone).
Incentives/rewards are often useful; punishment and criticism should be avoided.

Transabdominal electrical stimulation was found helpful in one small trial for treating children with slow-transit constipation, including reduced soiling, with effects lasting more than two years for one third of the patients; symptoms recurred within 6 months in another third.

Anal plugs may be helpful for a selected group of people either as a substitute for other forms of management or as an adjuvant treatment, but limited data are available. Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 studies found a 35% drop-out rate with short-term "pseudo-continence" achieved by some of those who continued to use plugs.

Physical therapy for in children with pelvic floor dyssynergia (defined as an inadequate coordination of the pelvic floor muscles) was found to be helpful in the management of fecal incontinence resulting in a decrease or elimination of fecal incontinence in the majority of subjects in a retrospective chart review of 64 patients. Findings were in-line with adult-based studies.
Consultation with a pediatric gastroenterologist is necessary for treatment failure or when there is concern for organic disease (see Differential Diagnosis for clinical features).
Disimpaction treatments described in Table 1 in the chapter on constipation in children remain useful in hospital setting.

Limited evidence suggests consideration of hospitalization for difficult fecal removal and subsequent detailed examination for possible intestinal motility disorders in children whose colonic diameters measure greater than 5.5 cm.

Childhood constipation continues beyond puberty in up to one-third of patients. B
Twenty-four percent of children with functional non-retentive fecal soiling do not outgrow their encopresis during puberty and 15% still experience encopresis when reaching adulthood. B

A prospective observational study from Europe included 240 children with bladder or bowel dysfunction, some with neuropsychiatric developmental disorders. The authors concluded that these children had more severe baseline symptoms, and showed significant less improvement over one year.
